overview.title: 📖 Overview: From 'Priests, Too' to the Verse's Every Word
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 4a–4b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by continuing the 'isn't it obvious?' pattern for priests: they must cancel their Temple service to hear the Megilla, and they form a zimun even while eating sacrificial meat meant for atonement, since the Torah still calls it 'eating and being satisfied.' The mishna's own inclusion of priests in arakhin is then debated through ben Bukhri's position that priests are exempt from the half-shekel — could that exempt them from valuations too? From there the Gemara turns to the verse of arakhin itself (Leviticus 27:2, 'a vow of persons... according to your valuation') and mines it for a cluster of derashot: an unspecified vow's minimum payment, valuation of the whole body rather than a limb, inclusion of vital organs and of women as valuators and valuated, exclusion of the dead and the dying, and — spilling into the next daf — whether a tumtum who consecrates only his head thereby consecrates his whole self.

slides.title: 🕎 Priests: Obligated Even During Service
slides.subtitle: Three more 'isn't that obvious?' questions, three resolutions
rows: Their Temple service seems to take priority
Rav Yehuda/Shmuel: priests, Levites, and Israelites all cancel their service to come hear it
Eating sacrificial meat is atonement, not a social meal
Deuteronomy 8:10 'eat and be satisfied' makes it a meal requiring zimun regardless
Per ben Bukhri, priests are exempt from the half-shekel — perhaps also from valuations
The mishna teaches priests are included in arakhin regardless of ben Bukhri's view

slides.title: ⚖️ Must Priests Give the Half-Shekel?
slides.subtitle: Ben Bukhri's testimony at Yavne, and why it matters for arakhin

lines.speaker: Ben Bukhri
lines.text: I testify: any priest who contributes the half-shekel is not considered a sinner — implying priests are not obligated to give it at all.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan b. Zakkai
lines.text: Not so! Any priest who does not give the half-shekel is a sinner. Priests only excuse themselves by reading 'every meal offering of the priest shall be wholly consumed' as applying to the omer, the two loaves, and the showbread they would then partly own.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The mishna's inclusion of priests in arakhin is needed only per ben Bukhri — one might think 'your valuation... shekel of the Sanctuary' links arakhin to the half-shekel obligation.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: That verse isn't about priests at all — it teaches that no valuation may be assessed below a sela! The real concern is elsewhere: since priests are not redeemed as firstborns, maybe they're excluded from arakhin too.

lines.speaker: Rava/R' Ashi
lines.text: Rather, the concern was from 'he shall be set before the priest' — implying a priest is not set before another priest for valuation. The mishna teaches: priests ARE included nonetheless.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: Every possible verse that could have excluded priests from arakhin gets raised and dismissed in turn — the mishna's plain inclusion of 'priests' turns out to answer several distinct doubts at once.

slides.title: ❤️ What Does the Plural 'Persons' (נְפָשׁוֹת) Teach?
slides.subtitle: One word, read for several different halakhot

nodes.content: ❓ The verse reads 'a vow of PERSONS' — why the plural, and what does it add beyond 'valuation'?

columns.label: A vital organ
columns.content: One might exclude valuing a limb the soul depends on — 'nefashot' teaches: pay the FULL valuation regardless

columns.label: The dying (גוֹסֵס)
columns.content: 'He shall be set...and valued' — only one who CAN stand is valuated; the dead and the dying are both excluded

nodes.content: 💡 The same plural also teaches: one who valuates a hundred people pays for each of them; a woman may valuate or be valuated exactly as a man; and a repulsive man or one with boils is included despite having no market value
✅ One word, five distinct halakhot — the Gemara debates exactly which derivation truly needs the plural form

slides.title: 📜 Two Halakhot Hiding in 'According to Your Valuation'
slides.subtitle: בְּעֶרְכְּךָ is read twice, for two separate rulings

boxes.title: Unspecified Valuation (עֵרֶךְ סָתוּם)
items: One who vows 'a valuation is upon me' without naming anyone pays the SMALLEST fixed sum — three shekels (a girl under five)
Not fifty (the largest): 'if you grasped a lot, you grasped nothing; if a little, you grasped it'
Dispute: is that three-shekel sum reduced for a poor person, or fixed regardless of means?

boxes.title: Valuation of the Whole Self
items: One gives the value of his ENTIRE body, never of an isolated limb
If one vows 'the valuation of my hand is upon me,' he owes nothing — the vow attaches only to a whole person

slides.title: 🐴 Consecrating 'The Head' — Whose Body Is Really Sanctified?
slides.subtitle: Rava and Abaye debate a tumtum's limb-vow against parallel cases

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava: a tumtum, though excluded from arakhin, IS included in 'assessment' (דָּמִים) via 'then your valuation shall be' — and if he consecrates one limb, he is 'judged by its dignity': his whole self becomes hekdesh
2️⃣ Abaye objects from a baraita: saying 'this SLAVE's head is hekdesh' makes the treasury a partner in the whole slave — but 'this DONKEY's/COW's head is hekdesh' sanctifies only the head itself
3️⃣ Abaye's proof: a donkey and cow aren't included in arakhin at all, yet their 'head' case still isn't governed by 'judged by its dignity' — so the rule can't track inclusion in arakhin

4️⃣ Rava counters: by that logic, a slave — who IS included in arakhin — should also be 'judged by dignity,' yet only his head becomes hekdesh too! Resolution: it depends on whether the consecration is for the altar (head alone) or for Temple upkeep (the whole)

summary.principle: After extending the 'obviously obligated' pattern to priests hearing the Megilla, forming a zimun over sacrificial meat, and being valuated despite ben Bukhri's exemption from the half-shekel, the Gemara turns to the arakhin verse itself and shows that its plural 'nefashot' and the phrase 'according to your valuation' each carry multiple, independently necessary halakhot.

flowSteps.content: 🕎 Priests need explicit inclusion: cancel service for Megilla; form zimun over sacrificial meat; included in arakhin despite ben Bukhri's half-shekel exemption
❤️ 'Persons' (נפשות) teaches: full value for a vital-organ vow; exclusion of the dead and dying; payment per head for a hundred; women included; repulsive/boil-afflicted included

columns.content: 📜 'According to your valuation' also fixes the unspecified vow at 3 shekels and requires valuing the whole self, not a limb
🐴 Tumtum's 'head is hekdesh' vs. slave/donkey/cow cases — altar-consecration vs. Temple-upkeep consecration

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: no clause of the arakhin verse is redundant — the Gemara insists each phrase, and each doubled or plural form, must justify its own distinct halakha

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, why does a baraita need to state that priests are obligated to hear the Megilla?
o: Because priests are generally exempt from time-bound mitzvot
To teach that priests, Levites, and Israelites all cancel their Temple service to come hear it
Because only women were originally obligated to read it
Because the Megilla may only be read inside the Temple
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that priests at their service, Levites on their platform, and Israelites at their watches all cancel their duties to hear the Megilla — a real halakha, not an obvious one.

quiz.q: What was Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's response to ben Bukhri's claim that a priest who gives the half-shekel is not a sinner?
o: He fully agreed with ben Bukhri
He said any priest who does NOT give the half-shekel is a sinner; priests merely excuse themselves via an interpretation of the verse about the priestly meal offering
He ruled that only the High Priest must give it
He said priests are exempt from all Temple-related gifts entirely
quiz.e: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai held that priests ARE obligated in the half-shekel, and that priests who avoid it do so only by (mis)reading the verse about the wholly-burnt priestly meal offering.

quiz.q: How much must one pay who vows an 'unspecified valuation' (עֵרֶךְ סָתוּם) without naming a particular person?
o: Fifty shekels, the largest fixed valuation
One shekel
Three shekels, the smallest fixed valuation — that of a girl under five
Whatever amount he personally decides
quiz.e: The baraita rules he pays the smallest of the Torah's fixed valuations, three shekels, following the principle that a lesser, certain amount is preferred over a larger, uncertain one.

quiz.q: What does 'he shall be set before the priest, and the priest shall value him' teach about a moribund person (goses)?
o: A person who cannot stand — whether dead or dying — is excluded from the halakha of valuation
Only the fully dead are excluded; the dying are still valuated
The dying must be valuated at half the normal sum
The verse has no bearing on the dying at all
quiz.e: The Gemara derives that anyone included in the category of 'standing' is included in valuation, and anyone who cannot stand — the dead and the dying alike — is excluded.

quiz.q: In the baraita about declaring 'the head' of an animal or slave hekdesh, what distinguishes a slave's case from a donkey's or cow's?
o: There is no distinction between them
Declaring a slave's head hekdesh makes the treasury a partner in the ENTIRE slave, while for a donkey or cow only the head itself becomes hekdesh
Only a cow's head can ever be consecrated this way
A donkey can never be declared partly consecrated
quiz.e: The baraita rules that 'the head of this slave is hekdesh' sanctifies the whole slave in partnership, whereas 'the head of this donkey/cow is hekdesh' sanctifies only the head — Rav Pappa explains this is because an ox's head is sold separately in the butcher shop.
